title: N-Digit Primes With Most Frequent Digit D
statement:
You are given two integers `N` and `D`. Find all `N`-digit prime numbers whose **most frequent digit** is `D`, and print them in increasing order.

A prime has `D` as its most frequent digit when the digit `D` appears in it at least as many times as any other digit. If several digits tie for the highest count, each of them counts as a most frequent digit, so the prime is included when `D` is one of them. For example, for `N = 2` and `D = 3` the answer is `13 23 31 37 43 53 73 83`: in `13` the digits `1` and `3` each appear once, so `3` is a most frequent digit, while `33` is not prime and `29` has no `3` at all.

Numbers never have leading zeros, so an `N`-digit number lies between `10^(N-1)` and `10^N - 1` (for `N = 1` that is `1` to `9`). If no such prime exists, print `-1`.
inputFormat: A single line containing two integers `N` and `D`.
outputFormat: Print the qualifying primes in increasing order, separated by single spaces, on one line. Print `-1` if there are none.

examples.explanation: Among the two-digit primes, those that contain at least as many 3s as any other digit are 13, 23, 31, 37, 43, 53, 73 and 83. In each of them the digit 3 appears once and no digit appears more than once.
The one-digit primes are 2, 3, 5 and 7. None of them contains the digit 1, so nothing qualifies.

For three-digit primes the digit 1 must appear at least as often as every other digit. For example 101 has two 1s, 113 has two 1s, and 127 has one 1 tied with 2 and 7, while 103 has 1, 0 and 3 each once, so 1 ties for the most frequent digit.

hints: Testing every N-digit number with trial division repeats a lot of work. Which classical algorithm lists all primes up to a bound at once?
Run a sieve of Eratosthenes up to 10^N - 1 and then only look at the primes that have exactly N digits (at least 10^(N-1)).
For each prime count how often every digit occurs. Keep it when the count of D equals the maximum count over all digits (and is at least 1).
